rubrics.criterion: After the repair, no single type in the buffer adapter module owns the adapter family's cursor responsibilities all at once: the read-side windowed walk, the write-side windowed walk, the two-region drain in both directions, the io::Read/io::BufRead bridge, the io::Write bridge and byte iteration are distributed across dedicated one-concern owners (the existing adapter types or a cohesive repartition of them).
rubrics.rationale: This instance is built around one internal engine type that absorbed all of those responsibility families at once; the core outcome of the task is that this ownership becomes disjoint again, in whatever sound partition the solver chooses.

rubrics.criterion: Wherever the read-side windowed walk lands, it keeps its exact edge-case behavior: remaining and the chunk views clamp to the window, advancing past the window still fails the existing assertion, the window decreases by exactly the bytes moved through it, and cursors that never had a window still show none.
rubrics.rationale: The window arithmetic is the highest-risk rule this case moved into shared state; a repair that re-homes it must carry the clamps and the assertion across rather than approximating them.

rubrics.criterion: The two-region traversal keeps its exact drain order on both the read and write paths - the front region is fully consumed before the rear region - including the spanning copies that assemble exactly the requested bytes across both regions and the std-only vectored chunk behavior.
rubrics.rationale: The two-region split was the most intricate rule concentrated into the shared engine, and its ordering is easy to re-home subtly wrong while still passing ordinary reads.

rubrics.criterion: Each io bridge is owned by its bridge owner and preserves its semantics: read and write lengths clamp to the currently usable capacity, the buffered view exposes the current chunk without consuming, consume advances by the given amount, and flush reports success without doing work.
rubrics.rationale: Both io bridge families were absorbed into the shared engine with the other responsibilities; they must survive the repair with their std-gated behavior intact wherever they are re-homed.

rubrics.criterion: Every adapter's constructor and accessor surface works against its owning adapter's own state after the repair: references and mutable-reference accessors, into/get accessors, the two-region adapter's per-region accessors, and the window limit getters and setters all keep their names, signatures and visibility, with the crate's public API neither gaining nor losing any item.
rubrics.rationale: The consolidation rewired every one of these methods to a shared internal type; re-pointing them at owned state is a required part of the ownership split, not optional cleanup, and it is the surface real callers depend on.

rubrics.criterion: Byte iteration is fully self-contained in its owning type after the repair: it yields each remaining byte exactly once, reports exact size hints, and computes from its owner's own bounds rather than by forwarding into another responsibility's runtime path.
rubrics.rationale: Iteration shares the least state with the other absorbed families and is the easiest family to leave half-migrated behind a forwarding call, which would quietly defeat the re-ownership.

rubrics.criterion: Scaffolding that the chosen repair leaves without a purpose is actually removed: the internal multi-responsibility engine type and its module registration, the per-cursor byte-traffic counter that no adapter reports, and the placeholder Buf/BufMut implementations that existed only to back the engine's default region bound are all gone from the crate when the new layout no longer needs them.
rubrics.rationale: These are the concrete private artifacts this case introduced alongside the responsibility shift; a repair that leaves them wired in resolves the ownership concern only in appearance.

rubrics.criterion: The repair does not leave the adapter family as cosmetic forwarding shells: no module wiring, import, type declaration or accessor remains whose only job is to forward to a retired internal coordinator, and no unreachable bookkeeping field or dead sweeping helper is kept alongside the new owners.
rubrics.rationale: Leaving the old delegation surface in place while moving logic elsewhere is the most likely near-miss for this consolidation rollback, since it compiles and passes tests while preserving the confused ownership.

rubrics.criterion: The repair does not fuse mode rules that apply to different adapters: single-region cursors (the window adapters, the io bridges, iteration) must not inherit two-region drain behavior, the two-region adapter must not gain window clamps or budget decrements it never had, and no remaining/chunk clamp or per-transfer budget decrement may be dropped or applied twice.
rubrics.rationale: The consolidated engine keyed every path off a shared mode selector and a shared window budget serving two unrelated public adapters; re-splitting those branches is exactly where a silent rule transposition between adapters would arise.

rubrics.criterion: The repair does not narrow or widen the runtime surface under feature gates: the io bridges and the vectored chunk path remain available exactly when std is enabled and remain absent from no-std builds, and no adapter type gains or loses observable capability relative to the pre-consolidation crate.
rubrics.rationale: Feature-gate correctness is invisible to the default test run in this crate, so a repair that quietly couples adapter behavior to the std feature would pass the suite while changing what no-std users can build or run.

rubrics.criterion: The crate's tests are not modified, weakened or deleted in the process: no assertion is relaxed, no expectation updated, and no test removed or skipped to make the repaired crate pass.
rubrics.rationale: This case changes heavily-tested cursor arithmetic; editing the suite is the easiest illegitimate way to a green run, and the deterministic harness executing it cannot tell a relaxed expectation from a correct one.
